details:
**Tashlikh (tashlich)**
An afternoon ritual, usually on the first day of Rosh Hashanah, in which observers throw bread crumbs or pebbles into a river, stream, or other body of water to symbolically cast away their sins. It is based on Micah 7:19 ("You will cast all their sins into the depths of the sea") and is the single most common clue for the holiday.

**Shofar**
A ram's horn blown during Rosh Hashanah services, traditionally 100 times each morning (it is not blown when the holiday falls on Shabbat). The blasts include the tekiah (one long blast), shevarim (three broken blasts), and teruah (rapid staccato blasts), and they are meant as a call to spiritual awakening and repentance.

**Apples dipped in honey**
The signature food of Rosh Hashanah, eaten in hopes of a "sweet new year." Other symbolic foods include pomegranates (sometimes said to have 613 seeds, matching the 613 commandments) and carrot tzimmes; some avoid nuts because the gematria of the Hebrew word for nut (egoz) equals that of the word for sin (chet).

**First of Tishrei**
Rosh Hashanah falls on the first (and second) day of the month of Tishrei, the start of the civil year in the Hebrew calendar. It is the first of the High Holy Days and comes nine days before Yom Kippur on the tenth of Tishrei.

**Days of Awe (Yamim Nora'im) / Ten Days of Repentance**
The ten-day penitential period that begins on Rosh Hashanah and ends on Yom Kippur, devoted to teshuvah (return or repentance). The Avinu Malkeinu ("Our Father, Our King") prayer is recited throughout this period.

**Book of Life (Sefer Hachaim)**
According to tradition, God opens the Book of Life on Rosh Hashanah and inscribes each person's fate for the coming year, but the judgment is not sealed until Yom Kippur. This gives rise to the holiday greeting wishing someone to be "inscribed and sealed" for a good year.

**Yom Teruah**
The biblical name of the holiday ("Day of Shouting" or "Day of Blasting"), referring to the sounding of the shofar commanded in the Book of Numbers. Other alternate names are Yom HaZikaron ("Day of Remembrance") and Yom HaDin ("Day of Judgment").

**Jewish New Year**
Rosh Hashanah literally means "head of the year." It commemorates the creation of the world, and observers greet each other with "Shana tova" ("a good year"). Questions about New Year's celebrations in general often mention it alongside Nowruz and Chinese New Year.

**Selichot**
Penitential prayers recited in the days leading up to Rosh Hashanah (during the preceding month of Elul for Sephardim, and starting the Saturday night before the holiday for Ashkenazim). They ask God for forgiveness ahead of the season of judgment.

**Machzor**
The special prayer book used on Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur in place of the everyday siddur. It contains the extended holiday liturgy, including a lengthened repetition of the Amidah prayer.

**Piyyutim and Unetanneh Tokef**
Piyyutim are liturgical poems added to the High Holy Day services. The most famous is Unetanneh Tokef, which describes God judging all creatures and deciding "who shall live and who shall die" in the coming year.

**Binding of Isaac (Akedah)**
The Torah readings for Rosh Hashanah are the birth of Isaac (Genesis 21) on the first day and the Akedah, Abraham's near-sacrifice of Isaac (Genesis 22), on the second day. The ram caught in the thicket in that story is linked to the use of a ram's horn as the shofar.

**Uman pilgrimage**
Breslov Hasidim travel each year to Uman, Ukraine, to spend Rosh Hashanah at the grave of their founder, Rabbi Nachman of Breslov. Tens of thousands of pilgrims make the journey.

**Fast of Gedaliah**
A minor fast day observed on the third of Tishrei, the day after Rosh Hashanah ends. It mourns the assassination of Gedaliah, the Jewish governor of Judah after the Babylonian conquest.

**Shana tova cards**
Greeting cards sent for the new year, popularly called "tovas." The Israeli artist Haggai is known for the images and light verses he created for them.
